title: Qualitative diode I-V: equilibrium, forward, reverse

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A diode's current–voltage curve is asymmetric because of what bias does to the barrier. In equilibrium the built-in barrier makes diffusion and drift cancel. **Forward bias** (p side positive) lowers the barrier, so diffusion wins enormously: majority carriers flood across and become minority carriers on the other side. The current grows exponentially with voltage.

**Reverse bias** raises the barrier. Diffusion is shut off and only a tiny drift current of minority carriers that stumble into the depletion region flows. It is set by how many minority carriers exist, not by the voltage, so it saturates at a small value. That is why a diode conducts one way and blocks the other.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Forward bias lowers the barrier from \(\varphi_{bi}\) to \(\varphi_{bi} - V_D\).
Minority concentration at the edge rises by a Boltzmann factor:
\[ p_n(x_n) = p_{n0}\,e^{V_D/V_{th}} \]
Each 60 mV of forward bias raises the current about 10×.
Reverse current \(\approx -I_S\), nearly independent of \(V_D\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Think of the current in decades. Suppose a diode carries \(1\ \mu\mathrm{A}\) at some forward voltage. Raise the bias by 180 mV: that is three 60 mV steps, so the current rises by \(10^3\) to about 1 mA. Lower it by 180 mV and the current drops to about 1 nA. In reverse, the current would bottom out at \(-I_S\) no matter how hard you push.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Thinking forward bias makes the depletion region wider. It narrows.
- Believing reverse current grows with reverse voltage (until breakdown it does not, ideally).
- Saying the forward current is mostly drift; it is diffusion of injected minority carriers.
- Treating "0.7 V" as a fixed property. It is just where the current becomes noticeable.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: To turn this picture into numbers you need the excess-carrier and continuity skills, which give the minority profiles at the depletion edges and then the ideal diode equation.
